messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 56
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Oceania
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Detective
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by caregiver (childhood)
  pcl5: 62

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Olfactory Danger Cue: Burnt smell, Victim Similarity: People who look similar to the victims, Positive Emotion Confusion: Positive emotions
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Similar Clothes: avoid wearing similar clothes, Memory Detachment: I detach myself from the memories, Avoid People: avoid other people
  Threat: Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience, Sleep Vigilance: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert, Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard
  Memory: Cannot Explain Clearly: When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish, Rage on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense rage, Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning
  Negative Appraisals: Shattered Beliefs: My beliefs about how the world works have been completely destroyed, Bad Coper: My reactions since the event show that I am a lousy coper, Character Blame: The event happened to me because of the sort of person I am

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Mika grew up in a house where danger announced itself before anyone spoke. His stepfather would come in from the garage smelling of singed metal and burnt oil, and Mika learned as a boy that the odor meant he should go still, watchful, ready for the blow or the grabbing hand. The abuse was physical and unpredictable, often set off when his stepfather had been drinking and tinkering with tools, and what stayed with Mika most was not a neat sequence but fragments: the smell, a shirt front close to his face, the heat of rage in his own body, the certainty that no one was coming to stop it. Even now, when he tries to explain what happened, he loses the thread and trails off, jaw tight, as if the story breaks apart under him.

He became a detective decades later, a job that had seemed to fit the version of himself that could stay hard, observant, and hard to surprise. But the work also keeps putting him near the kinds of cues that catch him off guard. In interviews with injured children or vulnerable adults, it is often the face of someone who resembles the child he once was that hits him first. At fire scenes or in shabby apartments with scorched pans, the burnt smell can pull the whole memory back without warning. The reaction is immediate and bodily: a rush in his chest, clenched muscles, a sense that he has to move or strike. When that happens, he does not think of it as remembering; it feels as if the past has broken into the room.

Those moments have shaped the habits of his adult life. On cases where a victim’s age, expression, or frightened posture resembles his younger self, Mika shortens the interaction or hands it to a colleague when he can. He keeps his distance from people generally outside work, telling himself it is easier that way, and since his divorce he has let that harden into a routine of going home alone and staying there. He is oddly particular about clothes, avoiding shirts and jackets that resemble what he remembers from that house, as if certain cuts or fabrics could make him feel too close to that boy again. He calls it being practical, but the logic is simple to him: if a smell, a face, or even a feeling of warmth and ease can open the trapdoor, then he has to narrow his world.

The effort to wall things off has not brought relief. When Mika feels a memory rising, he detaches from it, goes blank on purpose, pushes it away before it can fully form. Yet this seems to leave the past more jagged rather than less. Because he never stays with it long enough to put it into words, the memory remains in flashes that arrive with greater force, and when it does break through he is flooded with rage. The anger frightens him almost as much as the memory itself. He has come to see these reactions as proof that there is something fundamentally defective in him—that the abuse happened because of the kind of person he was, weak or marked somehow, and that the fact he still reacts this way means he is a lousy coper.

That belief has deepened over time because his body never stands down. He sleeps lightly and badly, lying awake as if some part of him still has to listen for footsteps in the hall. At work and in public he scans constantly, tracking voices, movements, exits. This permanent state of guard leaves him feeling that the world’s basic rules were shattered long ago, that safety is a story other people tell themselves. And when he notices how keyed up he is over something as small as a burnt smell from the break-room toaster, he reads it as more evidence of personal failure, not injury.

The loop has tightened in ways he can now see but not interrupt. The more he avoids certain people, clothes, and situations, the more unfamiliar ordinary contact feels, and even positive emotions have become confusing to him. A moment of warmth with a colleague, a brief sense of comfort, can feel dangerous in its own right, as if letting down his guard would invite harm; he becomes wary of the very states that might have connected him to others. That narrowing of his life leaves him alone with the fragments, and alone they return more abruptly. The repeated jolts of memory make him more watchful; the watchfulness makes burnt smells, familiar faces, and even good moments stand out as possible threats; and each new reaction seems to confirm his view that something is wrong with him at the core.

What finally brought Mika to treatment was an interview with a teenage assault victim who looked enough like him at that age that he felt himself go hot and lose the room. He had to leave, and afterward he sat in his car shaking, furious, and unable to give a clear account of why. For the first time, he worried his way of managing this was costing him the work he has built his life around. He says he wants help sleeping and “getting a handle on it,” but what frightens him most is the possibility that the past has fixed him permanently, and what he barely allows himself to hope is that these reactions might make sense without meaning he is ruined.
